title: Research Bite #51: A Cornerstone of Adaptivity -- A Meta-Analysis of the Expertise Reversal Effect
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #51 covers a meta-analysis by Leonard Tetzlaff, Bianca Simonsmeier, Tabea Peters, and Garvin Brod, 'A cornerstone of adaptivity -- A meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect,' published in Learning and Instruction (2025, Vol. 98, Article 102142). The team pooled 60 experimental studies and 5,924 participants (176 effect sizes total) to test the expertise reversal effect (ERE): the idea that instructional assistance (worked examples, scaffolding, guidance) helps novices but can actively hinder learners who already have domain knowledge. The meta-analysis confirms the effect is real and asymmetrical -- low-knowledge learners gain more from high assistance (d = 0.505) than high-knowledge learners lose from low assistance (d = -0.428) -- meaning the cost of over-scaffolding an expert is smaller than the cost of under-scaffolding a novice. Educational status and content domain both moderated the size of the effect, so the ERE is not uniform across ages or subjects. Barton's practical takeaway is that when a teacher is unsure of a class's prior knowledge, defaulting toward more assistance is the safer choice, and tools like intelligent tutoring systems offer a scalable way to track and adapt to individual knowledge levels in real time.
points: The meta-analysis's asymmetry finding -- assistance helps novices more than its absence helps experts -- gives teachers a practical tie-breaker rule: when in doubt about a class's prior knowledge, err toward providing more scaffolding rather than less.
Pooling 60 studies and nearly 6,000 participants gives this synthesis unusual statistical weight compared to any single classroom study of worked examples or scaffolding.
Educational status and content domain both moderate the ERE's size, meaning a one-size-fits-all scaffolding policy across year groups or subjects will systematically mis-serve some students.

The paper's framing of assistance as something to fade, not just apply, positions the ERE as a companion principle to worked-example research: the same support that accelerates a novice becomes a redundant, even harmful, crutch for an expert.

Intelligent tutoring systems are flagged as a practical route to operationalizing the ERE at scale, since they can track individual knowledge levels and adjust assistance dynamically -- something a single teacher cannot do continuously for 30 students.
quotes: This article presents a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (ERE), a phenomenon where instructional assistance benefits novices but hinders experts. The researchers conducted a systematic literature search, including 60 experimental studies with 5924 participants, to evaluate the ERE's strength and identify moderators.

Their findings confirm that low-knowledge learners benefit significantly from high assistance, while high-knowledge learners perform better with low assistance. The study also highlights that the ERE is asymmetrical, with providing assistance to novices having a stronger positive impact than withholding it from experts.
Educational status and content domain were found to moderate these effects, suggesting varied applicability across different learning contexts and age groups.

If teachers remember one thing, it should be to adjust instructional methods based on learners' domain knowledge. Novices benefit significantly from high assistance, while experts learn better with low assistance. Critically, providing assistance to novices has a stronger beneficial impact than withholding it from experts, so when in doubt, it's better to provide assistance.

Utilise tools for adaptation: Intelligent tutoring systems are a promising option for designing instruction aligned with the Expertise Reversal Effect, as they can track and adapt to learner knowledge levels in real time.
